title: He Never Believed in the Paranormal. After Renovating a Haunted Victorian Home, He's Now a 'Believer' (Exclusive)
excerpt: John Ryan, 36, Florida-based designer, talks with PEOPLE about his experience renovating a historic mansion on HGTV’s ‘A Very Haunted Renovation’
content:
NEED TO KNOW

  • Designer John Ryan lived in the 1898 Bihl Manor for six weeks while filming HGTV's A Very Haunted Renovation

  • Renovating historic homes can cost hundreds of thousands, with hidden issues like plumbing and electrical quickly draining budgets

  • Ryan says paranormal experiences in the home changed his outlook and influenced the renovation to honor its Victorian history

A historic home already comes with its own personality. From the creaking woodwork to the hidden details beneath centuries-old carpet, every room tells a story.

For John Ryan, a Florida-based designer and cast member on HGTV's A Very Haunted Renovation, the house at the center of the series came with a presence that couldn't be explained.

"It was like a home that you see in a horror movie," Ryan tells PEOPLE exclusively. "There's just this eerie feeling about it… It was straight out of a movie."

But the 36-year-old designer wasn't simply visiting the house; he was living and competing inside it as the cast filmed for roughly six weeks, spending 13 to 14 hours a day on set while sharing the historic property with five other designers.

"It was tough, like I've never experienced that before in my life," he says. "For me to move into a house with six other designers and live with them, eat with them, sleep and share one bathroom and just have my norm be broken was probably the most frightening thing."

The Bihl Manor house was built in 1898 and had sat vacant long enough for its underlying issues to become as daunting as its terrifying atmosphere.

Still, for a roughly 4,000-square-foot home like this Victorian Manor, the biggest expenses are rarely the ones a homeowner gets to show off.

"All of the interior stuff — the necessities, the plumbing, the electrical," he explains, can quickly drain a budget. "You don't know those costs until you're in there, ripping down walls and then seeing what's in there."

This could mean discovering rodents had damaged wiring or realizing the original cast-iron plumbing has deteriorated.

"Let's say you just have to redo the entire electrical [and] the entire plumbing, you're looking at a couple hundred thousand dollars," he says.

In other words, someone who enters an old-house renovation with a $250,000 budget may spend most of it on work that is essential, but entirely invisible once the walls are closed back up.

The historic charm also comes with a price tag when it is time to replace doors and other period-appropriate details.

"You're gonna want some good solid wood doors, and wood is like gold," he says.

For an entire set of solid interior doors designed to suit an 1800s Victorian home, he estimates homeowners could spend roughly $35,000 to $40,000.

Then, there are permits, which Ryan estimates can cost several thousand dollars and add months to a project timeline.

"If I pull a permit, let's say, in the city of Boca, I'm waiting about three, four months before I'm even approved," he says. "So you have to budget your time in for the approval process."

Material costs can make an already ambitious budget even more precarious.

Ryan estimates that tariff-related surcharges can add "between like 8 percent and as high as 20 percent" to the cost of building materials and furniture, with 15 percent serving as an average.

"It's always changing," he says, noting that some companies list the surcharge separately while others simply fold it into a higher overall price.

Still, he believes certain original details are worth preserving whenever possible, especially flooring.

"If you have a beautiful wood staircase, don't carpet it [and] don't rip it out," he says. "Refinish it and just let the original wood shine."

Installing new wood flooring throughout a home of that scale can cost approximately $50,000 to $60,000, including materials and installation, according to Ryan.

Refinishing and sealing existing floors may land closer to $25,000 to $30,000. It is still a major investment, he acknowledges, but one that can retain a home's irreplaceable character.

"Things back then were beautiful and done properly," he says.

Yet for all the practical surprises behind the walls, some of the show's most memorable moments involved something no renovation or budget could anticipate.

Ryan says he arrived at the Bihl Manor open-minded, but not especially spiritual. He believed ghosts could exist in theory, he says, but had never encountered anything like it.

"The first thing that I really noticed was just the shift in temperature," he says. "It was cold, and you'd walk through these different parts of the home and you can just feel it. I mean, it was wild."

During the first week, the experience became so draining that Ryan questioned whether he could stay. "There were at least three or four times where I'm like, 'I can't do this, like I need to go,'" he recalls.

"I just felt drained; my energy was just not there."

As the cast began using paranormal-investigation tools and learning more about the home's former owners and their children, Ryan says the atmosphere and his own outlook began to shift.

"We did some REM pods," he says. "It was wild, because I've never experienced that. I don't know if I've ever really believed in it, but I mean, I'm a believer now."

The experience ultimately influenced the renovation itself. "We learned a lot of information about the owners of the house and their children and what that house over the years has been," he says.

"I think we did a great job sticking to the whole Victorian era." As for the home's unseen residents? "We left the spirits very happy," he says.

A Very Haunted Renovation airs new episodes on Tuesdays at 8:00 PM ET on HGTV.
